newsitem.title: DUBAI: Petrol price war breaks out in Saudi Arabia.
newsitem.headline: Petrol price war breaks out in Saudi Arabia.

text.p: A retail price war has erupted at gasoline stations in oil giant Saudi Arabia despite government warnings, Saudi newspapers reported on Tuesday.
The winners of the forecourt wars are Riyadh motorists who are now filling up thir tanks at a cost that would be the envy of heavily tax-burdened drivers in the West.
"Despite official warnings from the government, the price war is still very much on in the capital," the English language Arab News newspaper said.
Some Riyadh petrol station owners have slashed the price of leaded petrol to the equivalent of 14 U.S. cents a litre, two cents a litre below the government retail price.
Arab News called the development as a "savage price war".
Saudi motorists have grown accustomed to cheap gasoline and diesel from the world's largest and most prolific oilfields.

Petrol prices have traditionally been held below world market levels by the Saudi government to encourage economic growth and urbanisation. But the government is unlikely to welcome any rise in local oil demand caused by lower pump prices.

Riyadh removed part of the subsidy on domestic petroleum prices last year in an attempt to cap rising local demand which had reached double-digit annual growth rates, threatening to cut the country's oil export potential.

Rising electricity demand forced state oil company Saudi Aramco to cut its crude exports by up to five percent in August to supply fuel-hungry power stations meeting demand for summer air conditioning.
Petroleum exports are the economic backbone of Saudi Arabia -- the world's largest crude producer and exporter -- pumping $40 billion a year into the state coffers.

Rising petrol demand could cut into the kingdom's 60,000 barrels per day (bpd) of high-value gasoline exports and divert more of the country's daily output of eight million bpd into the domestic refining system and away from world markets.
The price dicounting has already forced five filling stations to close in the eastern part of the city because of the struggle for customers, the Arabic Al-Eqtisadiah newspaper reported.
